sandhi.type: no change (final m before a vowel); anusvāra before the next word
sandhi.note: Final m stays m before the vowel of अशिवम् and is simply written on to it; the m of अशिवम् becomes anusvāra before the ś of शिवदूती. Inside the compound, अट्ट + अट्टहास gives अट्टाट्टहास by अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101).
After ai the visarga (as रु) stands as r before a vowel: शब्दैरसुराः. Then the visarga of असुराः becomes s before the t of त्रेसुः.
Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra, twice.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (its second member अट्टहास, ‘loud laughter’, is itself a karmadhāraya: अट्टः हासः)
samasa.sense: a roar of laughter, laughter heaped on laughter
samasa.alt: The doubling of अट्ट may also be read simply as intensive repetition; the sense, an unbroken peal of loud laughter, is the same.

samasa.sense: the name given to the Śakti of Caṇḍikā who sent Śiva as her envoy (8.23–28)

morph.note: Perfect, 3rd plural, of √त्रस्. Beside the reduplicated तत्रसुः the grammar allows, for this root, the form with e in place of the root vowel and no reduplication (त्रेसुः), as in पेतुः from √पत्.
Perfect of √या: reduplicated य-या, and roots ending in ā take -au in the 1st and 3rd singular (ययौ, like दधौ).
Perfect of √कृ with reduplication च-कार (k → c in the reduplicated syllable) and vṛddhi of the root vowel in the 3rd singular.

mantras.anvaya: शिवदूती अशिवम् अट्टाट्टहासं चकार ह। तैः शब्दैः असुराः त्रेसुः, शुम्भः परं कोपं ययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses: Śivadūtī’s laughter (object अट्टाट्टहासम्, verb चकार), its effect on the asuras (instrument तैः शब्दैः, verb त्रेसुः), and on Śumbha (कोपं परं ययौ).
mantras.lit: Śivadūtī let out an ominous peal of loud laughter. By those sounds the asuras trembled; Śumbha went into extreme anger.
mantras.tr: Śivadūtī broke into a terrible, rolling laughter. At that sound the asuras shook with fear, and Śumbha flew into a towering rage.

comm.t: The last of the great sounds of the battle (9.19–23): the Goddess’s conch, bowstring and bell, the lion’s roar, Kālī’s blow on the earth, and now Śivadūtī’s laughter. Sound is a weapon here: it breaks the asuras’ nerve before any blow.
Śivadūtī is the Śakti that came out of Caṇḍikā’s own body in 8.23 and sent Śiva to Śumbha and Niśumbha as her envoy; 8.28 gives the name. Her laughter already felled asuras in 8.38 (चण्डाट्टहासैः).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same name, शिवदूती (name 405). The shared name points to a shared Śākta memory of this episode; the two texts remain distinct works.

sandhi.note: A word-final n before t becomes anusvāra + s: -n t- → -ṃst-. Here it is the n of a vocative.
a + i → e. The same change gives जयेति in the second line.
a + a → ā.
जय + इति → जयेति; the final i of इति becomes y before the a of अभिहितम्.
After ai the visarga stands as r before a vowel.

samasa.sense: wicked one — a standard term of abuse for the asura
the gods watching the battle from above

morph.note: Perfect of √हृ with the prefixes वि + आ (वि + आ → व्या by yaṇ): reduplication ज-हार (h → j in the reduplicated syllable) and vṛddhi of the root vowel. वि-आ-√हृ is the idiom for ‘to utter, speak’.

Past passive participle of अभि + √धा: the root धा takes the form हि before the -त of the participle (हित). Neuter singular without a subject: the impersonal passive, ‘it was called out by the gods’ = ‘the gods cried’.
Imperative of √जि (stem जय- with guṇa), used as an acclamation: ‘Be victorious!’, ‘Victory!’

mantras.anvaya: (हे) दुरात्मन्, तिष्ठ तिष्ठ इति अम्बिका यदा व्याजहार, तदा आकाशसंस्थितैः देवैः जय इति अभिहितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A correlative sentence: यदा … व्याजहार (when Ambikā spoke) and तदा … अभिहितम् (then the gods cried). Each clause quotes a cry closed by इति; the second is an impersonal passive with its agent in the instrumental.
mantras.lit: When Ambikā called out, ‘O evil-souled one, stop, stop!’, then ‘Victory!’ was cried by the gods standing in the sky.
mantras.tr: When Ambikā cried, ‘Stand, you wicked one, stand!’, the gods watching from the sky called out, ‘Victory!’
mantras.tr_note: The impersonal passive (‘was cried by the gods’) is turned into an active verb.

comm.t: The Goddess challenges Śumbha in the words the asuras themselves use in battle (तिष्ठ तिष्ठ, as in 2.64), and the gods answer her with the cry जय. Heaven and the battlefield speak at the same moment.
The gods in this carita are onlookers who invoked her (5.9 onward) and cannot fight; their part is to praise. Their cry anticipates the full hymn they will sing in chapter 11 once Śumbha is dead.

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (अतिभीषणा is itself a prādi compound: अतिशयेन भीषणा)
samasa.sense: a dart wrapped in flames, dreadful to see

samasa.vigraha: वह्नेः कूटम् वह्निकूटम्; वह्निकूटस्य आभा इव आभा यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose radiance is like a heap of fire
samasa.sense: blazing like a pile of fire

morph.note: Absolutive of आ + √गम्: with a prefix the absolutive ends in -य (ल्यप्), and √गम् may drop its m before it (आगत्य beside आगम्य). Its subject is the agent of the main action, Śumbha, though Śumbha stands in the instrumental of the passive.
Feminine present participle of आ + √या (adādi). For roots of this class in ā the feminine may be formed with or without the nasal (यान्ती / याती); the text has आयान्ती.
Past passive participle of निर् + √अस् ‘to throw’: ‘thrown out, cast off’, here ‘repelled’. It is the main verb of the sentence.

mantras.anvaya: शुम्भेन आगत्य या ज्वालातिभीषणा शक्तिः मुक्ता, सा वह्निकूटाभा आयान्ती (देव्या) महोल्कया निरस्ता।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या शक्तिः … मुक्ता) names the dart; the main clause (सा … निरस्ता) says what became of it. Both verbs are passive participles; the one who repelled it is not named.
mantras.lit: The dart which, having come up, was released by Śumbha, exceedingly terrible with flames — that (dart), approaching, shining like a heap of fire, was repelled by a great firebrand.
mantras.tr: Śumbha came on and hurled a dart wreathed in dreadful flames. As it came, blazing like a mountain of fire, it was struck aside by a great firebrand.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Mountain of fire’ renders वह्निकूट, literally ‘a heap (or peak) of fire’.

comm.t: Śumbha’s first attack in this round: a burning śakti. The verse does not say who threw the great firebrand (महोल्का) that turned it aside; the context makes it the Goddess, who answers every weapon in these verses.
A śakti hurled at the Goddess is met and undone, as Niśumbha’s was in 9.13. The pattern of the whole battle is that nothing aimed at her reaches her.

flags.uncertain: The agent of निरस्ता is unexpressed; supplying the Goddess (देव्या) follows the context, not the words. महोल्का may be a weapon of hers or a meteor-like missile; the text does not say which.

samasa.type: upamāna-pūrvapada karmadhāraya (taken as ‘a roar like a lion’s’)
samasa.sense: by Śumbha’s war-cry, loud as a lion’s
samasa.alt: As a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, सिंहस्य नादः, ‘the roar of the lion’ — but शुम्भस्य then has nothing to depend on; the roar here is Śumbha’s.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (लोकत्रय)
samasa.literal: the interior of the triad of worlds
samasa.sense: all the space of the three worlds

samasa.alt: As ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, निर्घातस्य निःस्वनः, ‘the noise of a thunderbolt’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Past active participle in -तवत् (क्तवतु) of √जि, nominative singular masculine जितवान्. It serves as a finite past verb: ‘(it) overcame’. The object (Śumbha’s roar) is understood.
Past passive participle of वि + √आप्, agreeing with the neuter लोकत्रयान्तरम् as predicate: ‘was filled’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अवनीपते, शुम्भस्य सिंहनादेन लोकत्रयान्तरं व्याप्तम्; घोरः निर्घातनिःस्वनः (तं) जितवान्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: a passive one (लोकत्रयान्तरं व्याप्तम्, with the instrument सिंहनादेन) and an active one (निर्घातनिःस्वनः जितवान्) whose object is supplied from the first.
mantras.lit: By the lion-roar of Śumbha the interior of the three worlds was pervaded; a terrible thunderclap-sound overcame (it), O lord of the earth.
mantras.tr: Śumbha’s lion-like roar filled the whole expanse of the three worlds; but a dreadful crash like thunder drowned it, O king.
mantras.tr_note: ‘It’ and ‘but’ are supplied: जितवान् has no expressed object.

comm.t: Śumbha answers the Goddess’s challenge with a roar of his own, and is outmatched even in sound. Medhas turns to his listener (अवनीपते), King Suratha, as he does at moments of tension. Whose thunder it was is not said. Read with 9.19–23, where every sound of the Goddess’s side overwhelms the asuras, the crash is naturally hers; it could also be the crash of the firebrand of 9.25. The text leaves it open.

flags.uncertain: The source of the thunderclap (निर्घातनिःस्वनः) is unstated, and so is the object of जितवान्; the reading ‘overcame Śumbha’s roar’ follows the context.

sandhi.note: Final n becomes the palatal ñ before ś, and the ś then becomes ch: -n ś- → -ñch-. The same change gives तत्प्रहिताञ्छरान्.
Visarga before t becomes s; then -n ś- → -ñch- as above.
After ai the visarga stands as r before a vowel.
-aḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, a + u → o, and the following a is absorbed (avagraha).

samasa.sense: the arrows the Goddess shot (the pronoun stem तद् in a compound stands for any gender: here तया, the Devī)

morph.note: Perfect of √छिद्: reduplicated syllable चि (ch → c) with ch doubled to cch after it (चि-च्छेद), guṇa of the root vowel. One singular verb serves two subjects in two clauses (देवी … शुम्भः), each cutting the other’s arrows.
Distributive adverb from शत with the taddhita -शस्: ‘by hundreds’; सहस्रशः likewise ‘by thousands’.

mantras.anvaya: देवी शुम्भमुक्तान् शरान्, शुम्भः तत्प्रहितान् शरान्, उग्रैः स्वशरैः शतशः अथ सहस्रशः चिच्छेद।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel clauses share one verb (चिच्छेद) and one instrument (स्वशरैः उग्रैः): the Goddess cut Śumbha’s arrows, and Śumbha cut hers.
mantras.lit: The Goddess (cut) the arrows released by Śumbha, (and) Śumbha the arrows sent by her; they cut them with their own fierce arrows, by hundreds and then by thousands.
mantras.tr: The Goddess cut down the arrows Śumbha loosed, and Śumbha the arrows she sent, each with fierce arrows of their own, by hundreds and by thousands.
mantras.tr_note: The singular चिच्छेद is rendered once for both clauses, with ‘each’ supplied for स्व-.

comm.t: An archery duel in which the two sides cancel each other’s arrows in mid-air. For one verse Śumbha holds his own; the next verse ends it.
A modern reading: the evenly matched exchange shows how long a struggle can seem balanced — and how quickly it turns once the decisive blow comes.
